nodes.name: Oyamel fir
nodes.desc: A cloud-forest conifer of central Mexican mountains. Overwintering monarchs gather in its forests, and UNESCO says keeping the standing forest and its microclimates is the key management need.

nodes.name: Pines
nodes.desc: Pines share the mountain slopes with oaks between roughly 1,500 and 3,000 m, below the oyamel belt.

nodes.name: Oaks
nodes.desc: Oaks grow on the lower slopes of the reserve, alone or mixed with pine, and drop leaves and acorns that feed the forest floor.

nodes.name: Milkweed
nodes.desc: The only plant monarch caterpillars eat. It grows far to the north, and herbicide use on Corn Belt crops has destroyed much of it.

nodes.name: Pineapple sage
nodes.desc: One of many sages and wildflowers recorded around the reserve. Its nectar feeds monarchs, bees and hummingbirds.

nodes.name: Monarch butterfly
nodes.desc: Most of the eastern North American population overwinters in the reserve, clustered in oyamel forest. Caterpillars store toxins from milkweed, which makes adults foul-tasting to most predators.

nodes.name: Western honey bee
nodes.desc: Recorded around the reserve visiting sages, Bidens and fuchsia flowers for nectar and pollen.

nodes.name: White-eared hummingbird
nodes.desc: A very commonly recorded bird of the highland forests, feeding on nectar from sages and other flowers.

nodes.name: White-tailed deer
nodes.desc: Listed among the reserve's larger mammals. It browses shrubs and plants and is prey for coyotes and bobcats.

nodes.name: Mexican volcano mouse
nodes.desc: A burrowing rodent of high-elevation forest on the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, and a recorded prey of the dusky rattlesnake.

nodes.name: Black-eared mouse
nodes.desc: An omnivore of seeds and insects that tolerates milkweed toxins and eats monarchs in numbers at the overwintering colonies.

nodes.name: Black-headed grosbeak
nodes.desc: A winter bird at the colonies that tolerates monarch toxins well enough to eat them, though it must ease off periodically.

nodes.name: Mesquite lizard
nodes.desc: A common small lizard of the mountain forests that hunts insects.

nodes.name: Mexican dusky rattlesnake
nodes.desc: A small high-elevation rattlesnake whose recorded prey includes lizards, frogs and small mammals such as the volcano mouse.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: A scavenger and opportunist named among the reserve's birds, feeding on carrion and small animals.

nodes.name: Coyote
nodes.desc: Listed among the reserve's mammals. It hunts mice and deer and scavenges carcasses.

nodes.name: Bobcat
nodes.desc: A recorded cat of the area that preys on deer, mice and other small mammals.

nodes.name: Great horned owl
nodes.desc: Named among the reserve's wildlife. A night hunter of small mammals such as mice.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Mountain sun drives plant growth, while the forest canopy keeps the winter colonies cool and shaded.

nodes.name: Rain & cloud moisture
nodes.desc: Cool, humid summers and dry winters, with cloud-forest moisture, support the oyamel forest.

nodes.name: Soil & nutrients
nodes.desc: Volcanic mountain soils hold the nutrients that firs, pines, oaks and wildflowers draw up.

nodes.name: Fungi & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen needles, leaves, wood and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
